title_original: Photography and the Music Scene: Listening to the Image

blocks.text: In the street, two silhouettes advance, wearing studded belts, sunglasses, leather biker jackets and torn tights. Further on, a couple kiss, their mohawks and tattoos matching. In Dave Clarke’s photographs, on show until the end of September at Jardin21 in Paris, the compositions are raw, the monochromes contrasted, the grain powerful. Nicknamed “The Baron of Techno”, the DJ, producer and remixer has worked with Depeche Mode, The Chemical Brothers and Placebo. He first tried photography in his youth, borrowing his father’s old camera. “But film was expensive, and developing it even more so. So I spent my pocket money on 45s and tapes instead, because you could always ‘develop’ those live, without waiting for a result, or record over them if you got it wrong,” he continues.

An emblematic figure of the techno scene, he draws inspiration from “gothic atmospheres, monochrome punk, soundscapes”, travels to many cities and gladly gets lost on foot. These experiences once again lead Clarke toward visual experimentation, a new way of translating the emotions he feels through sound. But how do the two media feed each other? How do scene photographers manage to impose their aesthetic, their own writing, when they capture the essence of an artist whose work already exists? Passionate about music, Jessica Attia and David Fitt have, like Dave Clarke, made the music scene their favorite space of expression. In the whirl of concerts and festivals, in the studio right beside the performers, or simply around a street corner, they turn composers and their fans into their preferred subjects. They capture an atmosphere, a sensibility, while preserving their singularity. It is a balancing act they have learned to master.

“I see my music and my photography as art forms that come together and symbolize my interpretation of the world, my need to try to understand it. I would say music makes me want to shoot, and shooting lets me empty my hyperactive mind. It’s a kind of zen,” Dave Clarke explains. The link between the two media seems obvious to him: “Eyes and ears are connected to the brain, so trying to separate their creative processes almost seems like an oxymoron,” he admits.

For Jessica Attia too, music is a binding thread, a necessary source of inspiration for her visual research. “It is constantly present in my mind and always finds a place in my images,” she confides. A devotee of Polaroid and analog film, the young photographer has already had the biggest names of the scene in front of her lens, among them Billie Eilish, Post Malone and DJ Snake. Their universes differ, yet she approaches every encounter the same way: fully immersed. “I think there is a part of truth, a part of themselves in their music, even if it isn’t the whole of who they are. That is why, as an artist, I have to listen to everything, feel their compositions, understand their creation,” she continues.

It was by “hanging around concerts all the time” that David Fitt made a place for himself in the rock and metal scene. “When I started getting interested in it, a photographer lent me his second camera body so I could experiment. I gave the images to the bands and, little by little, I became known,” he recalls. He often initiates the meetings with the artists he photographs, and considers himself lucky: “I work 90% of the time with people whose music I love,” he says. It is a starting point that allows him to build ties with those he admires. “I feel very privileged to be a collaborator, a fan and a friend to them all at once,” he admits. For him, such prior knowledge is essential: when you are already steeped in an artist’s compositions, it becomes easy to summon them through images.

But how, as a photographer, do you resist the urge to disappear? How do you reconcile two artistic representations? For Jessica Attia, everything comes down to connection: “I want to draw them somewhere they don’t expect to go. That’s where my own vision can take over. If I fully respect their identity, my emotional filter kicks in once we’re in the same room. It’s a kind of sharing: their world and their energy through my prism,” she explains.

David Fitt, for his part, does extensive research, looks at existing visuals, discovers who made them and asks questions to grasp what the band wants. “I also tell myself that if they come to me, it’s so that I make their universe my own,” he admits. He aims to combine the aesthetic of his subjects with his own language. In the end, the pictures fit together like pieces of a puzzle from which a global identity emerges. In Jessica Attia’s work, nearly all the details vanish into the penumbra, chiaroscuros turn abstract, and blurs summon an atmosphere, a mood, rather than a constructed narrative. In David Fitt’s portraits, colored halos set the scene, and enhance or conceal bodies and features. It is a dark, dreamlike universe from which the artists emerge as spectral, almost fantastical figures. “You have to be able to feel the atmosphere visually, or at least the image should show a facet that the music doesn’t give us,” he concludes. “Putting a face to a name makes a project more human, deeper, more compelling, all the more so at a time when AI is sweeping in.”
